items: The Trump administration announced new restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips, requiring export licenses for shipments to certain countries and tightening controls on overseas data centers.
The rule aims to prevent sensitive technology from being diverted to China, particularly in light of recent scrutiny over Nvidia's operations and a scandal involving its CEO.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has faced criticism for export control oversight, is accompanying Trump on his trip to China, where further actions against China may be discussed.

WASHINGTON, USA – The Trump administration said on Monday, November 16, it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips from companies like Nvidia, tightening controls as President Donald Trump headed to China for talks with President Xi Jinping.

The effort by the Commerce Department to crack down on overseas data centers and chip smuggling comes amid growing scrutiny of whether the department has been doing enough to keep sensitive technology from China.

The new rule restricts shipments of advanced chips to data centers like those in Thailand and Malaysia, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models. It also imposes new requirements on overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes of computing power” to firms headquartered in China.

The rule was published days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after reports of an affair with a woman who worked at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centers and has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

The rule sends a message “that America is serious about closing dangerous export control loopholes China has been exploiting for years,” John Moolenaar, the Republican chair of the House Select Committee on China, said in a statement.

Trump is due to meet Xi on Thursday in Shenzhen, the southern Chinese city hosting this week’s APEC summit. Trump has previously threatened or imposed technology restrictions on Beijing ahead of high-level meetings.

The new rule identifies Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil as countries where advanced chips are at higher risk of being diverted to China. Shipments of covered chips to those countries now require a US export license.
Those requirements do not apply to US companies operating data centers in the five countries.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has faced criticism for his oversight of export controls on chips to China in the wake of the Nvidia scandal, is among administration officials joining Trump on the trip to Asia, a White House official said.

Senior White House officials have discussed whether Lutnick should be pushed out, Reuters reported last week. But Trump told reporters on Monday as he departed the White House for the trip to the Philippines and China that he has no plans to replace Lutnick.

More actions against China are likely in the works. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that four government agencies had favored putting Megaspeed on a trade blacklist but the Commerce Department, which was in charge, had not.
“It’s a different viewpoint. One wants to be friendly with China and one wants to have a blowup with China,” Trump said on Monday. “They both are acceptable but they are different views.”

Fueling chatter about the dispute, the Commerce Department said in a statement that the new rule was written by the Department of the Treasury and the White House’s National Security Council, which also directed its release.
Trump also said he would not mind seeing Huang return ‌as Nvidia CEO, adding his voice to calls for Huang’s reinstatement.
Megaspeed said in a November 15 statement that it complies with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including US export control requirements.

Kate Koren, a former Commerce official, said the rule announced on Monday would have a much bigger impact on China than adding a single entity to the Commerce Department’s trade blacklist, known as the “Entity List.”

“Nvidia and Jensen (Huang) himself were key drivers of the argument for selling chips to China as a strategy,” Koren said. “The revelations last week put that argument into question, and the pendulum is swinging in the other direction — towards tighter export controls.”

The rule requires overseas data centers that provide a significant volume of compute power to companies headquartered in China to obtain US export licenses within 90 days to continue the services or face future export restrictions.
It also restricts chip shipments to data centers with compute power above a certain threshold.
The license requirement will not apply to systems used by online retailers and social media companies, which the department said do not pose the same national security threat.
The new regulation also formally rescinds a Biden-era rule that limited global access to AI chips through licensing requirements.

The Commerce Department said in early 2025 that it would not enforce the rule, and that it would rescind and replace it. But it did not take action until Monday, allowing billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips to flow to data centers used by Chinese AI companies.
Nvidia, which strongly opposed the Biden regulation, declined comment on the new rule. – Rappler.com
